heading: What is an Operating System
subheading: The interface between user applications and hardware
description:
An Operating System (OS) is system software that acts as an interface between user applications and the computer hardware. It manages resources and provides services for the efficient and secure execution of programs.

**Primary functions:**
• **Process Management** — creating, scheduling, and terminating processes.
• **Memory Management** — allocating and deallocating RAM for running programs.
• **File System Management** — organizing, storing, and retrieving files on disk.
• **Device Management** — controlling and coordinating I/O devices like keyboards, monitors, and printers.
• **Security & Access Control** — protecting data and resources from unauthorized access.

**Types of Operating Systems:**
• **Batch OS** — jobs are grouped and processed sequentially without user interaction (e.g., payroll systems).
• **Multiprogrammed OS** — multiple programs reside in memory simultaneously, and the CPU switches between them to maximize utilization (e.g., Windows, UNIX).
• **Time-Sharing OS** — CPU time is divided among multiple users or processes in small intervals, giving the illusion of simultaneous execution (e.g., Multics).
• **Distributed OS** — multiple independent computers work together as a single system, sharing resources over a network (e.g., LOCUS).
• **Real-Time OS (RTOS)** — designed for applications where data must be processed within strict, guaranteed time limits (e.g., medical devices, flight control systems).

Examples of popular operating systems: Windows, macOS, Linux, Unix, Android, iOS.

heading: Process & Program
subheading: From static instructions to a running entity with its own memory and state
description:
A program is a set of instructions written in a programming language, stored as a file on disk. It is passive — it does nothing until it is executed.

A process is a program in execution. When you run a program, the OS loads it into memory and it becomes a process with its own resources. A process is divided into four memory sections:
• Text — the compiled program code (instructions).
• Data — global and static variables.
• Heap — dynamically allocated memory (grows upward).
• Stack — local variables, function parameters, and return addresses (grows downward).

Process States — every process moves through these states during its lifetime:
• New — the process is being created.
• Ready — the process is loaded into memory and waiting for the CPU.
• Running — the CPU is actively executing the process's instructions.
• Waiting (Blocked) — the process is paused, waiting for an event like I/O completion.
• Terminated — the process has finished execution.

The Process Control Block (PCB) is a data structure the OS maintains for each process. It stores the process ID, current state, program counter, CPU registers, memory allocation details, scheduling priority, and I/O status. The OS uses the PCB to track and manage every running process.

heading: Threads
subheading: Lightweight units of execution within a process
description:
A thread is the smallest unit of CPU execution. Every process has at least one thread (the main thread), and it can create additional threads that run concurrently within the same process.

What threads share within a process:
• Address space, heap memory, static data, code segments, file descriptors, global variables, and signal handlers.

What each thread has of its own:
• Program counter, registers, stack, and execution state.

Process vs Thread:
• A process has its own independent memory space. Creating a process is expensive (involves duplicating memory). Communication between processes requires IPC mechanisms.
• A thread shares memory with other threads in the same process. Creating a thread is lightweight and fast. Threads communicate directly through shared memory, but this requires careful synchronization to avoid data corruption.

Benefits of multithreading:
• Improved performance through parallelism on multi-core CPUs.
• Faster context switching compared to process switching.
• Better resource utilization — threads share the process's resources instead of duplicating them.
• More responsive applications — one thread can handle user input while another performs background computation.

heading: CPU Scheduling
subheading: How the OS decides which process gets the CPU and for how long
description:
CPU scheduling is the mechanism the OS uses to decide which process in the ready queue should be given the CPU next. The goal is to maximize CPU utilization, minimize waiting time, and ensure fairness among all processes.

Key scheduling algorithms:
• **FCFS (First Come First Serve)** — processes are executed in the order they arrive. Simple but can cause the convoy effect, where short processes wait behind a long one.
• **SJF (Shortest Job First)** — the process with the smallest burst time runs first. Gives the optimal average waiting time but requires knowing burst times in advance.
• **Round Robin** — each process gets a fixed time slice (quantum). After the quantum expires, the process is moved to the back of the queue. Fair and responsive, commonly used in time-sharing systems.
• **Priority Scheduling** — each process is assigned a priority, and the highest-priority process runs first. Can be preemptive or non-preemptive. Risk: low-priority processes may starve.
• **MLFQ (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)** — uses multiple ready queues with different priorities and time quanta. Processes can move between queues based on their behavior, balancing responsiveness for interactive tasks with throughput for CPU-bound tasks.

**Preemptive vs Non-preemptive:**
• Preemptive — the OS can interrupt a running process and give the CPU to another (e.g., Round Robin, Preemptive SJF).
• Non-preemptive — once a process gets the CPU, it keeps it until it finishes or voluntarily yields (e.g., FCFS, Non-preemptive SJF).

heading: Context Switching
subheading: Saving and restoring process state when the CPU switches between processes
description:
Context switching is the process of saving the state (context) of the currently running process and loading the saved state of the next process to be executed. It allows a single CPU to handle multiple processes by rapidly switching between them.

**What happens during a context switch:**
1. The OS saves the current process's context (program counter, registers, memory mappings) into its PCB.
2. The OS selects the next process from the ready queue using the scheduling algorithm.
3. The OS loads the saved context of the selected process from its PCB.
4. The CPU resumes execution of the new process from where it left off.

Context switching is pure overhead — the CPU does no useful work during the switch. The time it takes depends on hardware support, OS complexity, and the amount of state that needs to be saved and restored.

Why it matters:
• Too frequent context switching degrades performance because the CPU spends more time switching than executing.
• Too infrequent context switching makes the system less responsive.
• The OS must strike a balance — the time quantum in Round Robin scheduling directly affects how often context switches occur.

heading: Process Synchronization
subheading: Coordinating processes that share resources to prevent data corruption
description:
Process synchronization ensures that multiple processes or threads accessing shared resources do so in a controlled manner, maintaining data consistency and avoiding conflicts.

**Race Condition:**
A race condition occurs when the outcome of a program depends on the timing or order in which processes execute. If two threads read, modify, and write a shared variable simultaneously without coordination, the final result becomes unpredictable. This is one of the most common bugs in concurrent programming.

Semaphores:
A semaphore is a synchronization tool that controls access to shared resources using a counter and two atomic operations:
• wait() (P operation) — decrements the counter. If the counter becomes negative, the process is blocked.
• signal() (V operation) — increments the counter. If there are blocked processes, one is woken up.

Types of semaphores:
• Binary Semaphore — can only be 0 or 1. Used like a lock to protect a single resource. Functionally similar to a mutex.
• Counting Semaphore — can hold a value greater than 1. Used to control access to a pool of identical resources (e.g., a pool of 5 database connections).

**Mutual Exclusion:**
Mutual exclusion ensures that only one process can access a critical section (shared resource) at a time. It is the most fundamental requirement for correct synchronization.

heading: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
subheading: Mechanisms that allow processes to exchange data and coordinate
description:
IPC (Inter-Process Communication) refers to the mechanisms provided by the OS that allow different processes to communicate and share data with each other.

Common IPC mechanisms:
• Pipes — a one-way communication channel between two related processes. Data written by one process can be read by the other. Named pipes (FIFOs) allow communication between unrelated processes.
• Message Queues — processes send and receive structured messages through a queue managed by the OS. Messages are stored until the receiving process reads them.
• Shared Memory — the fastest IPC method. Two or more processes share a region of memory, allowing direct read/write access. Requires synchronization (e.g., semaphores) to prevent race conditions.
• Sockets — used for communication between processes on the same machine or across a network. A socket is defined by an IP address and a port number. Types include Stream Sockets (TCP, reliable) and Datagram Sockets (UDP, fast but unreliable).
• Signals — asynchronous notifications sent to a process to indicate that an event has occurred (e.g., SIGKILL to terminate a process).

**Cooperative vs Independent processes:**
• Independent processes do not share data and cannot affect each other.
• Cooperative processes share data or resources and need synchronization to work correctly.

heading: Deadlocks
subheading: When processes are stuck forever waiting for each other's resources
description:
A deadlock is a situation where two or more processes are permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource held by another process in the group. No process can proceed because none will release its resource until it gets the one it is waiting for.

Four necessary conditions (all must hold simultaneously):
1. Mutual Exclusion — at least one resource is held in a non-shareable mode.
2. Hold and Wait — a process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources.
3. No Preemption — resources cannot be forcibly taken away from a process; they must be released voluntarily.
4. Circular Wait — a circular chain of processes exists, where each process waits for a resource held by the next process in the chain.

Handling deadlocks:
• Prevention — design the system so that at least one of the four conditions can never hold. For example, enforce a resource ordering to eliminate circular wait.
• Avoidance — use algorithms like the Banker's Algorithm to check whether granting a resource request would lead to an unsafe state before actually granting it.
• Detection & Recovery — allow deadlocks to occur, detect them using resource allocation graphs, and recover by terminating processes or preempting resources.
• Ignorance (Ostrich Algorithm) — simply ignore deadlocks and assume they are rare enough not to matter. Used by most general-purpose operating systems like Windows and Linux.

Safe State: A system is in a safe state if there exists at least one sequence in which all processes can complete execution without causing a deadlock.

heading: Memory Management — Virtual Memory
subheading: Creating the illusion of unlimited memory using disk as an extension of RAM
description:
Virtual memory is a memory management technique that gives each process the illusion of having a large, contiguous block of memory, even if the physical RAM is much smaller. It achieves this by using disk space as an extension of main memory.

How it works:
• Each process gets its own virtual address space. The OS and hardware (MMU — Memory Management Unit) translate virtual addresses to physical addresses at runtime.
• Only the pages or segments currently needed are kept in RAM. The rest are stored on disk in a swap area.

**Logical vs Physical Address:**
• Logical (Virtual) Address — generated by the CPU during execution. This is what the program sees.
• Physical Address — the actual location in RAM. The MMU translates logical addresses to physical addresses at runtime.

**Paging:**
• Divides both virtual memory and physical memory into fixed-size blocks called pages (virtual) and frames (physical).
• Eliminates external fragmentation since all pages and frames are the same size.
• The OS maintains a page table for each process that maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers.

**Segmentation:**
• Divides memory into variable-size segments based on the logical structure of the program (e.g., code segment, data segment, stack segment).
• Each segment has a base address and a length.
• More intuitive for programmers but can cause external fragmentation.

**Static vs Dynamic Loading:**
• Static Loading — the entire program is loaded into memory before execution begins. Simple but uses more memory.
• Dynamic Loading — modules are loaded into memory only when they are called. Saves memory since unused code is never loaded.

heading: Demand Paging & Page Replacement
subheading: Loading pages on demand and deciding which pages to evict when memory is full
description:
Demand Paging is a technique where pages are loaded into memory only when they are actually needed during execution — not in advance. This saves memory and speeds up program startup.

**How demand paging works:**
1. The process tries to access a page.
2. If the page is in memory (valid bit set), execution continues normally.
3. If the page is not in memory, a page fault occurs.
4. The OS checks if the memory reference is valid. If not, the process is terminated.
5. If valid, the OS reads the required page from disk into a free frame in memory.
6. The page table is updated, and the interrupted instruction is restarted.

When memory is full and a new page needs to be loaded, the OS must evict an existing page. This is where page replacement algorithms come in:
• **FIFO (First In First Out)** — evicts the oldest page in memory. Simple but not always efficient.
• **LRU (Least Recently Used)** — evicts the page that has not been accessed for the longest time. Better performance but harder to implement.
• **Optimal (Belady's Algorithm)** — evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. Theoretically optimal but impossible to implement in practice since it requires future knowledge.

**Belady's Anomaly:**
A counterintuitive phenomenon where increasing the number of page frames actually increases the number of page faults. This happens specifically with the FIFO algorithm. LRU and Optimal algorithms do not suffer from this anomaly.

heading: Thrashing
subheading: When the system spends more time swapping pages than executing processes
description:
Thrashing occurs when the system is so overloaded with processes that it spends most of its CPU time on page swapping (moving pages between RAM and disk) rather than doing actual productive work.

How it happens:
1. Too many processes are loaded into memory, each getting too few page frames.
2. Processes frequently access pages that are not in memory, causing excessive page faults.
3. The OS spends all its time handling page faults — reading pages from disk and writing pages back — leaving almost no time for actual process execution.
4. CPU utilization drops dramatically even though the system appears busy.

How to detect it:
• Monitor CPU utilization. If CPU utilization drops while the degree of multiprogramming (number of processes) increases, the system is likely thrashing.

How to prevent it:
• Use the Working Set Model — track each process's working set (the set of pages it actively uses) and ensure enough frames are allocated to hold it.
• Locality of Reference — programs tend to access a small set of pages repeatedly in a short time period (spatial and temporal locality). Loading these pages together reduces page faults.
• Reduce the degree of multiprogramming — suspend or swap out some processes to free up memory for the remaining ones.
• Use better page replacement algorithms like LRU instead of FIFO.

heading: Kernel & System Calls
subheading: The core of the OS and how user programs request its services
description:
The kernel is the central component of the operating system. It is the first program loaded when the computer starts, and it remains in memory throughout the system's operation. It acts as a bridge between user applications and the hardware.

Kernel responsibilities:
• Managing CPU, memory, files, and processes.
• Scheduling which processes run and when.
• Facilitating communication between software and hardware.
• Controlling access to peripherals and I/O devices.

Types of kernels:
• **Monolithic Kernel** — all OS services (file system, device drivers, memory management) run in kernel space under a single address space. Fast due to fewer context switches, but a bug in any component can crash the entire system. Example: Linux.
• **Microkernel** — only the most essential services (IPC, basic scheduling) run in kernel space. Everything else runs in user space. More stable and modular, but slower due to frequent communication between user space and kernel space. Example: Minix.

**System Calls:**
A system call is the programmatic interface through which a user program requests a service from the kernel. It is the only way for user-level code to interact with hardware or perform privileged operations.

**User Mode vs Kernel Mode:**
• User Mode — the mode in which regular applications run. Programs cannot directly access hardware or memory of other processes. If they need system resources, they must make a system call.
• Kernel Mode — the privileged mode in which the kernel runs. It has unrestricted access to hardware, memory, and all system resources. When a system call is made, the CPU switches from user mode to kernel mode, executes the request, and switches back.

heading: Multiprocessing & Multiprogramming
subheading: Running multiple processes across multiple CPUs or on a single CPU
description:
Multiprocessing refers to running multiple processes simultaneously on a system with multiple CPUs or CPU cores. Each processor can execute a different process at the same time, genuinely in parallel.

Benefits of multiprocessing:
• Greater throughput — more tasks are completed per unit of time.
• Improved reliability — if one processor fails, the others can continue working.
• Cost-effective — multiple processors share the same memory, bus, and peripherals instead of needing separate systems.

**SMP (Symmetric Multiprocessing):**
A multiprocessor architecture where all processors are equal — any processor can execute any task, and they all share the same memory and OS. No single processor is the master. This is the most common multiprocessor design in modern computers and servers.

Multiprogramming is different — it refers to keeping multiple programs in memory on a single CPU so that the CPU always has something to execute. When one program is waiting for I/O, the CPU switches to another program. The goal is to maximize CPU utilization by eliminating idle time.

Key difference:
• Multiprogramming — one CPU, multiple programs in memory, CPU switches between them to stay busy.
• Multiprocessing — multiple CPUs, each executing a different process simultaneously for true parallelism.

heading: Starvation & Aging
subheading: When low-priority processes never get a chance to run, and how to fix it
description:
Starvation is a situation where a process is unable to get the resources it needs (typically CPU time) for an extended period because higher-priority processes keep getting served first. The starving process is technically ready to run but never gets scheduled.

Starvation commonly occurs with:
• **Priority Scheduling** — low-priority processes can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving.
• Shortest Job First (SJF) — longer processes may never execute if shorter processes continuously enter the queue.

Aging is the standard solution to starvation. It works by gradually increasing the priority of a waiting process over time. The longer a process waits, the higher its priority becomes. Eventually, even the lowest-priority process will have its priority raised high enough to be scheduled.

How aging works:
• Every process starts with its assigned priority.
• After each scheduling cycle (or fixed time interval), the priority of every waiting process is incremented by a small amount.
• Over time, a starving process's priority will surpass those of newer arrivals, guaranteeing it will eventually be scheduled.

This technique ensures fairness — no process is left waiting forever, regardless of its initial priority.

heading: Zombie Process & Cascading Termination
subheading: What happens when processes finish or their parents exit
description:
A zombie process (also called a defunct process) is a process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the process table. This happens because the parent process has not yet read the child's exit status using the wait() system call.

Key points about zombie processes:
• They do not consume CPU or memory resources — they are dead.
• They occupy a slot in the process table, which is a limited resource.
• If too many zombie processes accumulate, no new processes can be created.
• The parent must call wait() to read the exit status and clean up the zombie entry.
• If the parent process itself terminates without cleaning up, the zombie is adopted by the init process (PID 1), which periodically reaps zombie children.

Cascading Termination:
When a parent process exits, the OS may automatically terminate all of its child processes. This is called cascading termination. The rationale is that child processes are dependent on the parent, and allowing them to continue running without a parent could lead to orphaned processes consuming resources without oversight.

Not all operating systems implement cascading termination. In Unix/Linux, orphaned child processes are typically re-parented to the init process rather than being terminated.

heading: RAID Storage
subheading: Combining multiple disks for performance, reliability, or both
description:
RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) is a data storage technology that combines multiple physical hard disks into a single logical unit. The goal is to improve performance, increase storage capacity, provide fault tolerance, or a combination of these.

Common RAID levels:
• **RAID 0 (Striping)** — data is split across multiple disks for faster read/write speeds. No redundancy — if one disk fails, all data is lost. Use case: performance-critical applications where data loss is acceptable.
• **RAID 1 (Mirroring)** — data is duplicated on two disks. If one disk fails, the other has a complete copy. Use case: critical data that needs reliability (e.g., OS drive).
• **RAID 5 (Striping with Distributed Parity)** — data and parity information are striped across three or more disks. Can survive one disk failure. Offers a good balance of performance, storage efficiency, and fault tolerance. Most commonly used in servers.
• **RAID 6 (Double Parity)** — similar to RAID 5 but with two sets of parity data. Can survive two simultaneous disk failures. Use case: large storage systems where higher fault tolerance is needed.
• **RAID 10 (1+0)** — a combination of mirroring and striping. Data is mirrored first, then striped. Provides both high performance and high reliability, but requires at least 4 disks.

Less common levels:
• RAID 2 — uses Hamming code for error correction. Rarely used today.
• RAID 3 — bit-level striping with a dedicated parity disk.
• RAID 4 — block-level striping with a dedicated parity disk.

heading: Caching, Interrupts & Booting
subheading: Essential OS concepts — speeding up access, handling events, and starting up
description:
**Caching:**
A cache is a small, fast memory that stores copies of frequently accessed data from main memory. The CPU checks the cache first before going to RAM. If the data is found (cache hit), access is extremely fast. If not (cache miss), the data is fetched from RAM and a copy is placed in the cache for future use. Caching dramatically reduces average memory access time.

**Interrupts:**
An interrupt is a signal sent to the CPU by hardware or software indicating that an event needs immediate attention. When an interrupt occurs, the CPU pauses its current work, saves its state, and executes a special routine called the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) to handle the event. After the ISR completes, the CPU resumes its previous work.
• Hardware interrupts — triggered by devices like keyboards, mice, or network cards.
• Software interrupts — triggered by programs, often to request OS services (system calls).

**Bootstrap Program (Booting):**
The bootstrap program is the first code that runs when a computer is powered on. It is stored in ROM or firmware (BIOS/UEFI) and performs these steps:
1. Runs hardware diagnostics (POST — Power-On Self-Test).
2. Locates the OS kernel on disk.
3. Loads the kernel into main memory.
4. Transfers control to the kernel, which then initializes the system and starts user services.

**Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line):**
Spooling is the process of temporarily storing data in a buffer (usually on disk) so that a slower device like a printer can process it at its own pace. For example, when you print a document, the data is spooled to disk and the printer reads from it independently, freeing the CPU to continue other work.
